Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Anna Akhmanova as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in the review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Sean X. Sun (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

We all agreed that the revised version of the manuscript is much improved and clearly presents a very interesting and compelling story, well done!

Before the formal acceptance of the manuscript, one of the reviewers (rev. #1) made two final comments regarding (1) the contractile stress's role in volume control; and (2) the relative importance of membrane tension and voltage for the effects presented here. I think it might be a good idea to consider these comments and decide whether you think you can adapt the discussion part of the text so your points are clearly laid down.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have addressed my comments and the manuscript is much improved. I can recommend publication. I think there is generally no disagreement in our thinking of contractility and cell volume regulation. It is true that contractile force, or pressure, alone cannot really change the volume very much. This was already shown in Yellin et al., Biophys. J. 2018, and Li and Sun, Frontiers Cell Dev. Bio., 2022, and I agree with the authors' general thinking. However, the discussion in Pg. 7, I think, can be improved. Right now, it sounds like contractile stress is being compared with the total osmotic pressure of impermeable solutes inside the cell. But in reality, the contractile stress should be compared with the total osmotic pressure difference between inside and outside of the cell, which is much smaller than 100mM. During 10% volume change during cell spreading, I think since it's happening slowly (order of minutes), the ion flux and contractile stress should change simultaneously, possibly with contractile stress changing slowly, while ion flux happening very fast. But, the contractile stress must change, since at minimum, the cell is changing shape, and therefore cortical stress must change to maintain relative force balance. I'm still not completely sure whether is ok to neglect it, since the steady-state result of the proposed model is zero osmotic pressure difference between inside and outside, but in reality, there is about 1kPa of hydraulic pressure difference and 1kPa osmotic pressure (~0.5mM) difference. This difference may be small enough to be negligible in the current context. But it may not be small in other contexts, such as during cell motility.

The other issue I hope the authors can clarify in the discussion is the equal importance of membrane voltage and membrane tension in this story. Ion exchangers such as NHE and NaK are affected by both. The current dependence of exchanger flux with respect to voltage is based on just passing an ion through a constant electric field. This is generally not true for ion exchangers. I think most studies of ion exchangers show a voltage gating effect. This, after all, is the basis of action potentials. Therefore, these important facts should be clearly stated.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have made an effort to provide a detailed response to the reviewer's comments and the manuscript is of high quality to be published in Elife. The work presents a relevant step forward to understand the coupling of cell mechanics during cell spreading and volume regulation and opens up interesting questions to be addressed in future studies.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have completely addressed all my points, and I enthusiastically recommend publication.

results.result: At steady state, there is no strong correlation between cell spreading area and volume at the population level, independent of cell cycle stage. This was demonstrated across multiple cell types (HeLa, RPE-1, 3T3) using various measurement approaches including micropatterns and cell cycle markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C25 collectively demonstrate through multiple experimental approaches (RICM, FXm, micropatterns, cell cycle markers) that steady-state cell volume is not correlated with spreading area when controlling for cell growth. The data are consistent across cell types and measurement methods, with appropriate controls for cell cycle stage.

results.result: During cell spreading, cells undergo a transient volume loss of approximately 5% on average, occurring within the first 20 minutes, followed by volume recovery. This volume loss corresponds to water and ion loss while dry mass remains constant, as measured by FXm with 1% accuracy for individual cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 provide converging evidence from FXm volume measurements, quantitative phase imaging of dry mass, and control experiments on non-adhesive surfaces. The measurement precision and accuracy are well-characterized (C28-C29), and the interpretation that volume loss reflects water/ion loss is supported by the constant dry mass observation (C30).

results.result: Volume loss during cell spreading is correlated with spreading speed rather than absolute spreading area. Faster-spreading cells lose more volume and lose it faster, while slow-spreading cells show minimal volume loss. This relationship is independent of initial cell volume.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 establish the key finding that spreading kinetics, not final area, determines volume loss. The data show clear correlations between dV/dt and dA/dt (C35, Figure 1I), with both decreasing over time (C36), and no correlation with initial volume (C37). This is a central observation that motivates the mechanosensitive model.

results.result: Pharmacological perturbations of the actin cytoskeleton and myosin activity modulate spreading speed and correspondingly affect volume loss. Latrunculin A slows spreading and reduces volume loss (2-3%), while Y-27632 accelerates spreading and increases volume loss (10-15%). These effects are consistent across cell types and are due to altered spreading kinetics rather than direct drug effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C49 demonstrate that cytoskeletal perturbations affect volume loss through their effects on spreading speed. Key controls include Y-27 treated cells on non-adhesive surfaces showing no volume loss (C44), and similar effects across multiple cell types (C45). The MnCl2 experiment (C48) provides additional evidence by increasing spreading speed through a different mechanism.

results.result: Cells respond to osmotic shocks according to the classical pump-leak model, with fast volume changes (seconds timescale) followed by slower adaptation (minutes timescale). The Ponder relation is linear and independent of actin integrity or NHE1 inhibition, confirming accurate volume measurements and expected osmotic behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 validate the measurement system and establish baseline osmotic behavior. The Ponder relation matches literature values (C55), dry mass remains constant during volume changes (C54), and the response is independent of actin and NHE1 (C56-C57), all consistent with classical osmotic theory. This provides essential validation for interpreting spreading experiments.

results.result: Membrane tension, measured by tether pulling, is elevated during the spreading phase in fast-spreading cells (Y-27 treated) compared to control cells, while tension returns to similar levels at steady state. Non-spreading cells on micropatterns show low tension regardless of Y-27 treatment, suggesting spreading speed affects membrane tension.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 provide direct evidence for increased membrane tension during fast spreading. The key control showing low tension in non-spreading cells even with Y-27 treatment (C61) demonstrates the effect is spreading-dependent. However, tether force is an indirect measure of tension that also depends on membrane-cortex interactions, which should be acknowledged.

results.result: High temporal resolution osmotic shock experiments reveal volume changes occur on a seconds timescale with rates (~10 μm³/min for small shocks) similar to those observed during cell spreading. This timescale matching justifies using a mechanosensitive pump-leak model to explain spreading-induced volume changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C69 establish critical timescale information linking osmotic regulation to spreading. The comparison of rates between osmotic shocks and spreading (C68) provides quantitative justification for the modeling approach (C69). The observation of asymmetric permeability (C65) is noted but not fully explained, which is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: A mechanosensitive pump-leak model, where membrane tension modulates ion channel/pump activity, predicts the observed proportionality between volume loss and spreading speed without dependence on absolute spreading area. The model provides satisfactory fits to experimental data with physiologically reasonable parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 describe the core theoretical contribution. The model makes specific, testable predictions (C73) that match experimental observations. The fits shown in Figure 4D (C74) demonstrate quantitative agreement. The prediction that the mechanosensitivity parameter should be negative for physiological parameters (C72) is supported by detailed ion transport modeling in the appendix.

results.result: Cells possess large membrane reserves, with rupture occurring at 5.7-fold volume increase (3.3-fold surface area excess). Despite this excess, membrane tension can increase during fast deformation due to restricted unfolding when the membrane is bound to the cytoskeleton.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 address a potential concern about membrane availability. The rupture experiments (C75) provide direct evidence for membrane excess, consistent with literature (Ting-Beall et al., 1993; Guilak et al., 2002). The hypothesis about restricted unfolding (C77) is reasonable but remains somewhat speculative, as direct evidence for this mechanism is limited.

results.result: Inhibition of branched actin (CK-666) or NHE1 (EIPA) prevents volume loss during fast spreading induced by Y-27632, while GdCl3 treatment increases volume loss proportionally to increased spreading speed. None of these treatments significantly affect initial cell volume, indicating effects are specific to the spreading-induced mechano-osmotic coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 provide critical tests of the model's mechanistic predictions. The key finding that CK-666+Y-27 and EIPA+Y-27 combinations prevent volume loss despite fast spreading (C79, C83) strongly supports the mechano-osmotic coupling hypothesis. The control showing no effect on initial volume (C84) rules out general osmotic effects of the drugs.

results.result: When mechano-osmotic coupling is disrupted (Y-27+CK-666 or Y-27+EIPA), fast-spreading cells show the highest membrane tension during spreading, as predicted by the model. This confirms the model's validity and supports the existence of a membrane tension homeostasis mechanism that modulates volume to limit tension changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 provide strong validation of model predictions. The tether pulling experiments (C86) directly test the model prediction (C85) and show the expected pattern. The observation that tension is highest during spreading, not at steady state (C87), rules out drug artifacts. This represents compelling evidence for the proposed homeostasis mechanism.

results.result: Inhibition of Ezrin, a membrane-cytoskeleton linker, reduces volume loss during spreading despite similar or faster spreading speed. Electron microscopy confirms different spreading extents and branched actin perturbation in various conditions, with membrane structures present in all cases.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 provide additional support for the role of membrane-cortex coupling. The Ezrin inhibitor experiment (C98) is consistent with the model's assumptions about cortex-membrane interactions. The EM data (C99-C100) provide structural context, though quantitative analysis of membrane structures is acknowledged as challenging.

results.result: Model fitting reveals that for most conditions, the effective stiffness parameter varies by less than 30%, with volume loss explained by spreading speed differences. However, Y-27+EIPA and Y-27+CK-666 treatments decrease this parameter by an order of magnitude, suggesting branched actin networks are specifically required for mechano-osmotic coupling, possibly through direct association with ion channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 present an interpretation of model parameters that leads to a specific hypothesis about branched actin (C108). While the parameter analysis is sound (C104-C105) and the tether pulling data support continued tension generation (C106), the conclusion that branched actin is specifically required for the coupling (C108) is somewhat speculative. The proposed mechanism of direct actin-channel association (C109) is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Fast mechanical confinement induces actin-dependent volume loss (up to 30%) at nearly constant surface area in control cells, while Latrunculin A-treated cells maintain constant volume. Y-27632 treatment has no effect on confinement-induced volume loss, confirming contractility does not directly affect volume. This phenomenon is observed across multiple cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C115 demonstrate volume loss under ultra-fast deformation. The actin dependence (C110-C111), lack of contractility effect (C112), and constant surface area (C113) are well-documented. The observation across cell types (C114) strengthens generalizability. These experiments probe a different timescale regime than spreading.

results.result: Volume loss during fast confinement occurs within 30 milliseconds, involves only water/solute loss (not dry mass), and is too fast to be explained by the mechanosensitive pump-leak model. Imaging reveals transient streams of expelled fluid. While the mechanism differs from spreading, it also requires actin and is induced by membrane tension.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C120 characterize ultra-fast volume loss and appropriately acknowledge the model's limitations (C118). The millisecond timescale (C116), constant dry mass (C117), and visualization of expelled fluid (C119) are well-documented. The conclusion that the mechanism differs but shares some features with spreading (C120) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Dendritic cells migrating through collagen gels show volume fluctuations of a few percent, with faster-moving cells displaying larger fluctuations. The relationship between migration speed and volume variation coefficient is well-fitted by an extension of the mechanosensitive model, suggesting the mechano-osmotic coupling operates in physiological migration contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 extend the findings to a physiologically relevant context. The observation of speed-dependent volume fluctuations (C121-C122) and successful model fitting (C123) provide evidence that the mechanism operates during migration. The speculation about broader implications (C125) is appropriately tentative.

results.result: Cells modulate their volume depending on the rate of shape change, with slow deformation at constant volume and fast deformation leading to volume loss. This mechano-osmotic coupling, mediated by membrane tension effects on ion fluxes and dependent on actin cortex state, acts as a membrane tension homeostasis mechanism constantly at work in mammalian cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C91-C96, C126-C127 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all results. The rate-dependent volume modulation (C1-C2) is well-supported by spreading experiments. The mechanistic explanation involving membrane tension and ion fluxes (C3, C92) is supported by drug perturbations, tether pulling, and model predictions. The characterization as a homeostasis mechanism (C96, C126) is justified by the demonstration that volume loss limits tension increases.
